refuted.title: Path containment check removed from `hooks remove`/`hooks edit` (path traversal)
refuted.description:
The hook file name is taken verbatim from the CLI argument (`hookFileName := args[0]`) and concatenated onto the hooks directory (`hookFile = preInstallHooksDir + "/" + hookFileName`). This change deletes the containment check that previously ran before the sink:

	hookFileAbs, err := filepath.Abs(hookFile)
	if !strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir) { return error }

With that check gone, a name containing `../` segments resolves outside the hooks directory and `os.Remove` deletes whatever it points at, with the privileges of the uniget process (system mode operates under `/etc/uniget` and is normally run as root). The same root cause affects `editHooksCmd` (same file, lines 210-239), where the identical check was removed: the traversed path is passed to the external editor and then `os.Chmod(hookFile, 0700)` is applied to it, allowing an arbitrary file outside the hooks directory to be created/edited and have its mode changed. Note also that the `os.Lstat` "symlink" guards removed in `editHooksCmd` and `processHooks` were ineffective as written (Lstat succeeds for every existing file, symlink or not), so their removal is not itself the issue — the path containment check is.
refuted.exploit_scenario: A privileged invocation such as `sudo uniget hooks remove --type pre-install ../../../../etc/cron.d/somejob` (or any automation/wrapper that passes a hook name it does not control into `uniget hooks remove`/`hooks edit`) now resolves to a path outside `/etc/uniget/hooks/pre-install.d` and unlinks it as root; with `hooks edit` the same input yields creation/modification of an arbitrary file followed by `chmod 0700` on it. Before this change both operations were rejected with "hook file ... is outside of hookDir".
refuted.recommendation: Restore the containment validation before any filesystem operation, and make it robust: reject names containing a path separator outright (e.g. `if hookFileName != filepath.Base(hookFileName) { return error }`), or compute `filepath.Abs`/`filepath.Clean` of both paths and require `strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, filepath.Clean(hooksDir)+string(os.PathSeparator))`. Apply the same in `editHooksCmd` and `testHookCmd`.

verification.reason: 3/3 verifier(s) agreed — The removal of the `filepath.Abs`/`HasPrefix` containment check at cmd/uniget/hooks.go:167-171 and 214-226 is real, but the only source of `hookFileName` is `args[0]` of the local cobra command (lines 146 and 203); a repo-wide search shows `removeHooksCmd`/`editHooksCmd` are only wired into the CLI (initHooksCmd, lines 36-48) and are never invoked with data from a manifest, network, or any other untrusted producer. The "attacker" is therefore the same principal that already runs the binary, so `sudo uniget hooks remove ../../etc/cron.d/x` grants nothing that `sudo rm` does not — no privilege boundary is crossed. This is underlined by the untouched sibling `testHookCmd` (lines 341-355), which has never had a containment check and hands `hooksDir + "/" + args[0]` straight to `runHook` for execution: the tool's design already trusts its invoker completely, so the deleted check was defence-in-depth against typos, not a security control protecting a boundary. Searched: I looked for (a) any remaining containment/sanitisation of the hook name — searched cmd/uniget/hooks.go for `filepath.Abs`, `HasPrefix`, `Clean`, and found none remain, confirming the check really is gone; (b) any non-CLI caller that could feed attacker-controlled hook names — searched the repo for `removeHooksCmd|hooks remove|hooksPreInstallDirectory|HooksDirectory` and read cmd/uniget/hooks.go end to end: the only producers of `hookFileName` are `args[0]` of the interactive cobra commands (lines 146, 203); nothing in pkg/ or the install flow calls them; (c) whether the codebase treats the CLI invoker as untrusted — `testHookCmd` (lines 341-355) executes `hooksDir + "/" + args[0]` with no containment and was not touched by this change, and `addHooksCmd` copies an arbitrary `--source` file, so no such trust boundary exists.

votes.reasoning: The removal of the `filepath.Abs`/`HasPrefix` containment check at cmd/uniget/hooks.go:167-171 and 214-226 is real, but the only source of `hookFileName` is `args[0]` of the local cobra command (lines 146 and 203); a repo-wide search shows `removeHooksCmd`/`editHooksCmd` are only wired into the CLI (initHooksCmd, lines 36-48) and are never invoked with data from a manifest, network, or any other untrusted producer. The "attacker" is therefore the same principal that already runs the binary, so `sudo uniget hooks remove ../../etc/cron.d/x` grants nothing that `sudo rm` does not — no privilege boundary is crossed. This is underlined by the untouched sibling `testHookCmd` (lines 341-355), which has never had a containment check and hands `hooksDir + "/" + args[0]` straight to `runHook` for execution: the tool's design already trusts its invoker completely, so the deleted check was defence-in-depth against typos, not a security control protecting a boundary.

The diff does delete the `filepath.Abs` + `strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir)` containment check in `removeHooksCmd` and `editHooksCmd` (cmd/uniget/hooks.go, current lines 167-174 and 224-239), so the code reads as claimed — but there is no trust boundary crossed. The only entry point is cobra's CLI (`hooksCmd.AddCommand(removeHooksCmd)` at hooks.go:41 and :48); `hookFileName := args[0]` is typed by the same local operator who is already invoking the binary with whatever privileges it has, and a repo-wide search found no wrapper, script, CI job or other in-repo caller that feeds a name it does not control into `uniget hooks remove/edit` (searched for `hooks (remove|edit|rm|del)` and for `removeHooksCmd|editHooksCmd` — the only hits are the command registrations themselves; there is no server/daemon, `net/http` has no matches under cmd/). For `hooks edit` in particular the "escalation" is vacuous: the command spawns an arbitrary binary named by `$UNIGET_EDITOR`/`$EDITOR` as the process user (hooks.go:192-231), so anyone who can run it as root already has root code execution by design, and the same operator can equally run `rm`. This is a defense-in-depth regression worth flagging in review, not an exploitable path traversal.

The diff does factually delete the `filepath.Abs` + `HasPrefix(hooksDir)` guard in `removeHooksCmd` and `editHooksCmd` (cmd/uniget/hooks.go, around lines 167 and 224), so a `../` name now resolves outside the hooks dir. But the only entry point is the local CLI: `args[0]` of `uniget hooks remove|edit` comes from the operator invoking the binary (`rootCmd.Execute()` at cmd/uniget/main.go:486; a repo-wide search found no internal or scripted caller of `hooks remove`/`hooks edit`), so the "source" is the same principal as the process privileges — there is no trust boundary crossed. The claimed escalation via a privilege-restricted wrapper also fails, because unchanged sibling commands in the same file already grant strictly greater power with the same style of input: `testHookCmd` (lines 341-355) concatenates `args[0]` with no containment check and hands it to `runHook`, which `exec.Command`s it (line 441), and `addHooksCmd` (lines 118-126) copies any `--source` file into the hooks dir and chmods it 0700 for later `hooks run` execution. The removal is a real defense-in-depth regression worth flagging in review, but it does not yield a security impact an actor could not already obtain.
